caption:
Why do the rocks in Death Valley move by themselves?

They don't move alone. On Racetrack Playa in Death Valley National Park, rocks leave trails up to 100 m (330 ft) long, 3 to 12 inches wide and usually less than an inch deep. Tracks there have been studied since the early 1900s. The first documented account is from 1915, by a prospector named Joseph Crook of Fallon, Nevada.

In 1968 Bob Sharp and Dwight Carey tagged 30 stones and watched them for seven years. All but two moved. The smallest, "Nancy" — 2.5 inches across — travelled 260 m (860 ft) in total, including 201 m (659 ft) in a single winter. "Karen", an estimated 700 lb block of dolomite, never budged during the study and then vanished from the playa before May 1994. A geologist rediscovered it in 1996.

The answer arrived on 20 December 2013. GPS units and time-lapse cameras caught more than 60 rocks moving at once. Sheets of ice only a few millimetres thick, frozen on a shallow winter pond, break up on sunny mornings and are pushed by light winds, shoving rocks along at up to 5 m per minute. Some moves lasted 16 minutes. That ruled out the older idea of 90 mph gusts dragging rocks through mud.

What is still open: how long the phenomenon will last. Rock movement needs a flooded playa and freezing nights, and a statistical study by Ralph Lorenz and Brian Jackson suggests, at 4:1 odds, a decline since the 1960s–90s. Rocks have also been stolen, and in 2016 someone left 10 miles of tire tracks across the playa. That vandal was still unidentified in 2018.

Images by Romain Guy, Jon Sullivan, and Dan Duriscoe for the U.S. National Park Service. All public domain or CC0.
